title: Regular negative noun forms with singular owners
summary: Practise the regular singular partitive with singular owners.
targetSkills: Regular singular partitive in negative possession
objectives: Practise the regular singular partitive with singular owners.
Apply the pattern using the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Practise the regular singular partitive with singular owners.
When possession is denied, the thing uses a noun form called the partitive. For these eight regular nouns, add -a or -ä to the whole basic word.
Use -a when the word has a, o, or u; otherwise use -ä. Thus pallo → palloa, kynä → kynää, and neutral-only peli → peliä. This rule covers the regular nouns taught here.
keyPoints: Practise the regular singular partitive with singular owners.

examples.english: I do not have a ball.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Pallo has back vowels a/o, so add -a: pallo + -a = palloa. Keep the final o before the ending.
Put palloa (“a ball”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: You do not have a book.
steps: sinulla means “you as the owner” for one person. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Kirja contains the back vowel a; neutral i does not override it. Add -a: kirja + -a = kirjaa, keeping both adjacent a vowels.
Put kirjaa (“a book”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: She does not have a dog.
steps: hänellä means “he as the owner” or “she as the owner”; this example uses “she”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Koira contains back vowels o/a and neutral i. Add -a: koira + -a = koiraa; the two final a vowels remain.
Put koiraa (“a dog”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: I do not have a cat.
steps: minulla means “I as the owner”. Keep the supporting ei ole frame (“do not have” or “does not have”).
Kissa has back vowel a despite neutral i. Add -a: kissa + -a = kissaa; keep both final a vowels.
Put kissaa (“a cat”) after ei ole. The negative possession pattern calls for this singular partitive form.

examples.english: You do not have a pen.
steps: Sinulla names one listener as owner.
Keep ei ole.
kynä has only front vowels: kynä + -ä = kynää.

examples.english: He or she does not have a game.
steps: Hänellä names one owner without marking gender.
Keep ei ole.
peli has only neutral vowels: peli + -ä = peliä.

examples.english: He or she does not have a car.
steps: hänellä identifies the singular owner in this regular negative noun forms with singular owners pattern.
Use owner + ei ole; possession keeps the verb pattern fixed.
autoa (“a car”) is the complete regular singular partitive: auto + -a.

examples.english: I do not have a pillow.
steps: minulla identifies the singular owner in this regular negative noun forms with singular owners pattern.
Use owner + ei ole; possession keeps the verb pattern fixed.
tyynyä (“a pillow”) is the complete regular singular partitive: tyyny + -ä.

commonMistakes: After ei ole, use the partitive noun, not its basic form: palloa, rather than pallo.
Keep the final vowel when adding the ending: kirja + -a = kirjaa and kynä + -ä = kynää.
Choose the ending from the noun: back vowels take -a; front or neutral-only vowels take -ä in these regular words, including peli → peliä.
